explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Asa, the new king of Judah, did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God (2 Chronicles 14:2). That's how the writer sums him up before telling us what he did. Most of us would need a few extra paragraphs to explain ourselves.

Not quite, friend. The text says it flat out: "And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God." Asa is the new king of Judah, and the writer opens his reign with that line. It's a strong way to start a job.

explanations.answer: Seek the LORD and keep His law
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Asa commanded the people of Judah "…to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandments." Notice he doesn't just clear things out and walk away. He points the people toward the LORD. Clearing the shelf is half the job, and filling it with the right thing is the other half.

explanations.answer: Build a new temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: I see why a temple would come to mind, friend, but this passage never mentions one. What Asa commands is that the people of Judah seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and observe the law and the commandments. No blueprints, no hard hats. The command is about the people's hearts and their obedience.

Close to a war room, friend, but no. Asa does have an army, and verse 8 counts it, but the command here is different. He tells the people of Judah to seek the LORD and to observe the law and the commandments. Israel doesn't come up in these verses at all.

Right on, friend. "Because the land was at peace, Asa built fortified cities in Judah." Peace is the time he uses to build. That's like fixing the roof on a sunny day, and I bet nobody in Judah complained about it.

Fancy guess, baker, but the text doesn't call them royal cities. Verse 6 says Asa built fortified cities in Judah. That means cities with walls and strength, not a row of palaces. Fortified is the word the writer gives us.

Interesting pick, friend, but priestly isn't in the verse. Asa built fortified cities in Judah while the land was at peace (2 Chronicles 14:6). Then he talks about walls, towers, doors and bars (2 Chronicles 14:7). That's a city with its apron tied on tight, ready for whatever comes.

You got it, baker. "…the LORD had given him rest." Asa says the same thing to the people: "…He has given us rest on every side." (2 Chronicles 14:7). Rest is a gift here, and the text says who gave it. That's the kind of gift I'd happily unwrap twice.

Riches would be nice, friend, but that's not what the verse says. The LORD had given Asa rest, and that's why no one made war with him in those days. Asa repeats it to Judah: "…He has given us rest on every side." (2 Chronicles 14:7). I'd take a quiet stretch over a fat wallet any day.

Good word, baker, but not the one in this verse. Verse 6 says the LORD had given him rest, and that's why no one made war with him. Asa says it again to the people: "…He has given us rest on every side." (2 Chronicles 14:7). Wisdom is wonderful, but I'd say rest is the gift that lets a kingdom sleep in.

Hold on, friend, that one's not what Asa says. His reason is this: "The land is still ours because we have sought the LORD our God." He adds that the LORD has given them rest on every side. The army gets counted a verse later, but Asa never names it as the reason. He points to seeking the LORD.

That's right, baker. Asa tells Judah, "The land is still ours because we have sought the LORD our God." He doesn't brag about the army. He says the LORD has given them rest on every side. I'd say the king knows exactly where the credit goes.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the LORD his God
explanations.explanation: Exactly, baker. "Then Asa cried out to the LORD his God…" He has marched out and lined up in battle formation, and a million men are in front of him. Right there in the valley, he prays. That's a good lesson for me, because at a hard moment I'm more likely to stare at the ceiling.

explanations.answer: He sends messengers to ask for peace
explanations.explanation: Reasonable idea, friend, but the text doesn't say that. Asa has already marched out and lined up in battle formation in the Valley of Zephathah. Then "…Asa cried out to the LORD his God…" No messengers show up in this scene.

explanations.answer: He pulls his army back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That would be one way to go, baker, but it isn't what happens. The text says Asa marched out and lined up in battle formation near Mareshah. Then he cried out to the LORD his God. The army stays in the valley while he prays.

Yes, friend. Asa prays, "O LORD, You are our God. Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You." He's facing Zerah the Cushite, who leads that huge army. Asa speaks to the LORD plainly and gets right to it.

Not this time, baker. That line is in Asa's prayer: "Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You." He prays it while facing Zerah the Cushite and a million men. It's the last thing Asa says before the LORD acts.

Yes, baker. Asa prays, "Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You…" He also says, "…there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty." The people are lined up in the valley with their weapons, but the prayer rests on the LORD.

Those cities were a big project, friend, with all those walls and towers. But in his prayer Asa doesn't mention them. He says, "Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You…" The LORD is who Judah relies on.

The army was mighty, baker. Verse 8 even calls them mighty men of valor. But in the prayer Asa says, "Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You…" Asa prays that the LORD helps "…the powerless against the mighty." and that's who he's counting on.

explanations.answer: The LORD strikes them down and they flee
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. "So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled." The prayer ends and the LORD acts right away in the text. A million men, and the LORD is the one who handles it.

explanations.answer: They surrender and pay Asa tribute
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. There's no surrender in the text, and no tribute either. "So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled." They run away, and Judah chases them.

explanations.answer: They camp and wait for more troops
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but the Cushites don't stay put. After Asa prays, "…the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled." They're running, not waiting. There's no camp and no reinforcements in the text.

Not this time, friend. The text says the Cushites "…fell and could not recover, for they were crushed before the LORD and His army." They don't come back for another round. After the chase to Gerar, the text turns to Judah's plunder.

That's right, baker. "The Cushites fell and could not recover, for they were crushed before the LORD and His army." Nobody is coming back for round two. After the chase to Gerar, the text turns to Judah's plunder.

Yes, baker, terror is the word. The verse says, "…the terror of the LORD had fallen upon them." That's why Judah attacked all the cities around Gerar and plundered them, since there was much plunder there (2 Chronicles 14:14). I'd say that's a whole lot of fear landing at once.

Glory is a big, beautiful word, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. The verse says "…the terror of the LORD had fallen upon them." That's the reason Judah attacked all the cities around Gerar. The text uses terror here.

Nice word, baker, but the verse has a different one. It says the terror of the LORD had fallen upon the cities around Gerar. Because of that, Judah attacked them and plundered them. Wisdom doesn't show up in these verses.
